system.name: ChainCoder
system.one_liner: A program-synthesis language model that writes Python code in several passes from coarse to fine, using syntax-tree-derived subsequences as the prediction target.

content.variant_note: one real LeetCode solution redrawn in four identical code windows, each highlighting a different token class, then turned into tile rows and concatenated into one target strip
content.argues: Code is easier to generate when the target is reordered from outline to details: four syntax-guided subsequences, coarse to fine, are concatenated into one prediction target.
content.subject: A LeetCode solution split into four syntax-based subsequences and concatenated into one coarse-to-fine target token sequence.

encoding.color_means: One colour per subsequence, kept on the window glow, the boxed tokens, the tiles and the target segment: S1 = four band colours (orange extreme cases, yellow preprocessing, light green variable initialisation, blue core loop), S2 = bright green, S3 = light cyan, S4 = pink or magenta; dark green = special tokens BOS, PAD, EOS.
encoding.line_style_means: Black down arrows turn a window into a subsequence; pale coloured lines place a subsequence in the target; curly braces name coarse and fine stages; dark-blue boxes mark the tokens that belong to the subsequence (rest of the code stays pale).
encoding.shape_means: Small square tiles = tokens; ellipsis tile = omitted tokens; macOS-style window = code listing.
encoding.marker_means: S1-S4 name the four views, s with indices numbers the tokens of a subsequence, BOS, PAD and EOS are special tokens.
encoding.emphasis: The same code is repeated four times so that only the highlight changes, and the colour continues from window to tiles to the final strip, so the reader can trace where a part of the code ends up.

lessons.what_to_learn: Explain a data-formulation idea by redrawing one real example (here a code listing) in a row of identical windows, each highlighting a different token class in its own colour, then carry that colour onto the tiles and the final concatenated strip so the reader sees what ends up where.
lessons.suits: Methods that reorder, split or concatenate a sequence (code, text, tokens) into groups, where one concrete example can be recoloured per group.

evidence: We therefore construct the prediction target into four subsequences.
These four subsequences are concatenated by the system-level <PAD> token.

summary: ChainCoder generates Python code in several passes from coarse to fine. Figure 1 explains its prediction target on one LeetCode example, Merge Intervals. The problem text and the 16-line solution come first. The solution is then shown in four identical code windows, each highlighting a different part: coloured bands for the outline (extreme cases, preprocessing, variable initialisation, core loop), and boxed tokens for the core algorithm hint, the layout frame and the accessory tokens. Each window is arrowed (S1 to S4) to a row of colour-matched tiles, and pale lines place the four rows into one strip, joined by dark PAD tokens between BOS and EOS, with braces marking coarse and fine stages.
summary_zh: ChainCoder 把代码由粗到细分多遍生成。图 1 以 Merge Intervals 为例：同一段解法在四个窗口中分别高亮大纲、核心算法提示、布局框架和附属成分，得到 S1 到 S4 子序列，再用 PAD 拼成预测目标。
notes: The figure draws no model, only the data formulation. The pre-screen counted four panels (the four code windows); here they are four aligned columns of one drawing, so panel_count is 1 and the lanes field carries them. The code text sits inside bitmaps; the boxed tokens are vector boxes. Which token classes go into S2, S3 and S4 is read from the names under the tile rows and the paper text, not from the boxes alone.
